# Zero Trust Governance Principles

## Why CISA's cross-cutting capabilities — not another per-pillar tool — are what moves a program past Initial maturity

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**[Download this whitepaper as DOCX](zero-trust-governance-principles.docx)** — a Word copy of
this page, regenerated on every site deploy. (Also available from the
**Other Formats** link in the page sidebar.)
:::

### Executive summary

CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model (ZTMM) v2.0 defines five pillars — Identity,
Devices, Networks, Applications & Workloads, Data — each progressing through
four stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal. Most federal Zero Trust
programs read the model as a five-pillar shopping list, spend two-plus years
acquiring a point solution per pillar, and then stall at Initial or low
Advanced maturity. The reason is structural, and it is in the model itself:
CISA's ZTMM does not define maturity as five independent pillar scores. It
defines maturity as five pillars **operated through three cross-cutting
capabilities** — Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and
Governance — that run underneath and across all five. A program that fully
tools every pillar but never builds the cross-cutting layer cannot reach
Advanced or Optimal, because those stages are explicitly defined in terms of
continuous, automated, cross-pillar behavior — exactly what the cross-cutting
capabilities, not the pillar tools, are responsible for producing.

This paper sets out the governance principles that close that gap: what
specific adversary techniques these principles exist to defeat, why identity
is a necessary anchor but not a sufficient one — and why treating it as a
single, self-authenticating root of trust recreates the same failure mode
Zero Trust is supposed to retire — why privileged and administrative identity
need controls of their own, why continuous evidence is a governance property
and not a per-tool feature, why governance has to include enforcement and not
only visibility, and how the federal cloud-boundary constraints most agencies
operate under (GCC-class environments, TIC 3.0 boundary requirements) have to
be modeled explicitly rather than assumed away. It also makes a point that
gets lost as soon as an agency starts collecting per-vendor scorecards: **Zero
Trust has to be owned and assessed at the agency level, even though —
especially because — individual cloud service providers each offer their own
native assessment tool.** A CSP's own tool can only ever see its own platform;
the agency is the only party positioned to hold one Zero Trust posture across
all of them. None of this is vendor guidance — every claim traces to CISA,
NIST, OMB, and documented incident source material, cited throughout.

### 1. Why Zero Trust programs stall below Advanced

Three governance failure patterns recur across federal Zero Trust programs,
independent of which pillar tools an agency has bought:

**Pattern 1 — pillars are administered, not governed.** Each pillar gets an
owner, a tool, and a roadmap, but there is no shared authority correlating
decisions across them. An identity assertion evaluated in the Identity pillar
is not verifiable from the Data pillar; device posture from the Devices
pillar cannot be correlated with workload identity in Applications &
Workloads. Cross-pillar policy decisions degrade to the lowest common
denominator — usually a static allow-list — because no governance layer
resolves the pillars against each other.

**Pattern 2 — evidence is per-tool, not per-claim.** Each pillar's tool emits
evidence shaped by its own vendor's schema. Assembling that into a single
authorization narrative for a FedRAMP or Authority to Operate package is a
manual, point-in-time exercise, and it does not survive re-execution: the
tool's configuration has usually drifted since the evidence was captured, so
"re-run the audit" produces a different answer than the one on file.

**Pattern 3 — drift is discovered at audit time, not continuously.** Absent a
governance-level drift capability, the gap between declared policy and
runtime reality surfaces only when an assessor finds it — a Security Control
Assessment, a 3PAO review, or an incident. By then remediation is reactive,
and the agency has been carrying undisclosed risk for however long the drift
went undetected.

CISA's own ZTMM v2.0 Advanced and Optimal stage criteria call for exactly the
properties these three patterns block: continuous verification, automated
policy evaluation, and cross-pillar correlation. None of the three is
achievable by adding another per-pillar tool. They are, definitionally,
governance-capability work.

### 2. What Zero Trust actually defends against

Every principle in this paper exists to defeat specific, documented adversary
techniques — not to satisfy an abstract maturity model for its own sake.
Grounding the model in actual incidents matters because a governance program
that reaches every CISA maturity criterion on paper can still miss the
intrusion pattern it was meant to stop.

Four attack patterns motivate the principles that follow:

- **Identity-plane compromise at the root.** In 2023, a China-based actor
  tracked as Storm-0558 stole a Microsoft signing key and exploited a
  token-validation flaw to forge authentication tokens, reading email at
  roughly 25 organizations — including the U.S. Department of State and
  Department of Commerce — for weeks before detection. The federal Cyber
  Safety Review Board's subsequent report called the breach "preventable."
  This is the direct counter-example to treating identity as an
  unconditionally trusted root: when the root of trust is compromised, the
  blast radius is every relying party that trusted it, and it can happen
  without a single endpoint or network control ever firing. §4 and §5 return
  to this.
- **Hypervisor and virtualization-layer compromise that bypasses guest-OS
  telemetry entirely.** The February 2023 "ESXiArgs" ransomware campaign
  exploited a two-year-old, unauthenticated heap-overflow vulnerability
  (CVE-2021-21974) in ESXi's OpenSLP service, compromising thousands of
  internet-facing hosts before CISA and the FBI issued a joint advisory. In
  July 2024, CVE-2024-37085 — an ESXi Active Directory-integration
  authentication bypass — was exploited by multiple ransomware operators to
  gain full administrative control of domain-joined hypervisors by
  recreating a deleted "ESX Admins" AD group; ESXi trusted the group's
  *name*, not a verified, continuously-resolved identity. Both cases share a
  property no guest-OS-level Zero Trust control can see: the attacker never
  touches a monitored workload, because the hypervisor sits *beneath* every
  guest's telemetry. §9 returns to this directly.
- **Lateral movement through flat, VPN-reachable network segments.**
  Implicit trust granted by network location — a VPN tunnel, a flat virtual
  network, an unsegmented VLAN — is the mechanism, not an incidental detail,
  behind most large-scale ransomware and lateral-movement campaigns. It is
  the specific thing NIST SP 800-207 defines Zero Trust against.
- **Abuse of the governance and evidence layer itself** — an agency that
  names an owner and writes a policy but never wires in automated,
  preventive enforcement has built a reporting system, not a control. §7
  treats this as a first-class governance failure, not a footnote.

None of the principles that follow are abstractions from the ZTMM document
alone; each is a direct architectural response to one of these four
patterns.

### 3. The model most agencies read half of

[CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0](https://www.cisa.gov/zero-trust-maturity-model)
is usually summarized as "five pillars, four stages" — and that summary is
incomplete. The model explicitly layers **three cross-cutting capabilities**
underneath and across the five pillars: **Visibility and Analytics**,
**Automation and Orchestration**, and **Governance**. These are how an agency
operates the pillars at scale rather than by hand, and CISA's own stage
descriptions for Advanced and Optimal maturity are written in terms of these
capabilities, not additional pillar features.

| Cross-cutting capability | What it means operationally | Why pillar tooling alone can't provide it |
|---|---|---|
| **Visibility and Analytics** | A single, correlated view of signal across all five pillars — not five separate dashboards | Each pillar tool sees only its own pillar; correlation requires a layer that ingests all five |
| **Automation and Orchestration** | Policy decisions and remediation actions execute automatically, at machine speed, across pillar boundaries | Per-pillar tools automate within their own pillar; cross-pillar orchestration is, by definition, above any single tool |
| **Governance** | The authority and mechanism to set policy, hold every pillar accountable to a common standard, and — critically — enforce that standard automatically rather than only observe it | Governance is inherently a cross-pillar function; a tool can supply telemetry or even a policy engine, but the organizational authority to set the standard, and the mandate to enforce it, cannot be purchased as a product |

Of the three, **Governance is the capability most federal Zero Trust programs
shortchange** — not because no vendor sells governance-adjacent tooling (GRC,
CNAPP, and CSPM platforms all ship governance modules), but because none of
those tools substitutes for the organizational authority and enforcement
mandate governance actually requires. Budget and staffing default to pillar
tooling instead, in part because tooling is procurable and organizational
authority is not. The remainder of this paper is a set of concrete governance
principles for closing that gap — including, in §7, the distinction between
governance that merely observes and governance that enforces.

### 4. Principle one — identity is a necessary anchor, not a sufficient one

NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture*, defines the Zero Trust core logic
as a Policy Decision Point that evaluates subject identity **together with**
device state, resource sensitivity, and behavioral/environmental signals for
every access request. This is worth stating precisely, because it is
commonly compressed into "identity is the new perimeter." NIST 800-207 does
not rank identity as the supreme, self-authenticating signal above the
others; it requires continuous evaluation of *multiple* signals precisely
because no single signal, including identity, should ever be trusted
unconditionally. An architecture that treats a validated identity as
sufficient on its own — rather than as one input a policy engine continuously
re-evaluates alongside device posture and behavior — has rebuilt the old
perimeter model one layer up: an identity perimeter instead of a network one,
with everything behind a valid token or session inheriting trust the same way
everything behind a firewall once did.

Storm-0558 (§2) is the concrete demonstration of why this matters. The root
of trust was Microsoft's own token-signing infrastructure; when it was
compromised, every relying party that trusted a validly-signed token was
exposed, and the compromise was invisible to every control operating below
the identity layer. Centralizing trust in identity is still the right
architectural move — Pattern 1's cross-pillar correlation problem (§1) is
genuinely intractable without it — but centralizing trust also centralizes
risk, and a governance program that elevates identity architecturally
without also hardening it operationally has traded one single point of
failure for another.

OMB's M-22-09 makes the same structural point about identity's *priority*,
not its *sufficiency*: phishing-resistant MFA and enterprise-managed identity
are prerequisites the other pillars build on. The governance principle that
follows from both sources together:

**identity has to function as the addressing root the other pillars resolve
against, and that root has to be defended as the highest-value target in the
architecture — not treated as self-authenticating once established.** In
practice, this means both of the following are true at once:

- A device's compliance record should be *keyed to* an identity-plane
  object, not maintained in a separate device inventory reconciled by hand —
  this is the architectural half.
- The identity plane itself needs continuous access evaluation (re-checking
  session validity as conditions change, not trusting a token for its full
  nominal lifetime), short token lifetimes, hardware-bound or
  phishing-resistant credentials, and signing-key material protected in
  hardware (HSM-backed, with rotation and access logging) — this is the
  operational half, and it is not optional simply because the architectural
  half is sound. For the credential-family mechanics — which authenticator
  classes actually resist verifier impersonation — see
  [OrgComp Vol I Book 03, "Certificate-Based Authentication and
  Phishing-Resistant MFA"](../orgcomp-series/Vol_I_Book_03_OrgComp_Certificates_Tokens_Cryptographic_Identity.qmd).

This is the architectural reason the cross-pillar correlation problem in
Pattern 1 (§1) is tractable at all: if every pillar resolves against the
same identity plane, cross-pillar correlation reduces to *resolving identity
consistently*, which a governed identity plane already has to do. It is
also, unavoidably, the reason a compromise of that plane is catastrophic
rather than contained — which is precisely why §5 treats privileged and
administrative identity as a distinct principle rather than folding it into
this one.

### 5. Principle two — privileged and administrative identity is the highest-value target, and needs controls of its own

If identity is the addressing root (§4), administrative identity is the root
of the root: a Global Administrator credential, a hypervisor management-plane
admin, or a CSP account-root/organization-management identity has reach
across everything the identity plane touches. CVE-2024-37085 (§2) is the
sharpest available illustration of why this cannot be an afterthought: ESXi's
Active Directory integration trusted an AD group **by name**, not by a
continuously re-verified, non-recreatable identity — an attacker with
sufficient AD permissions could delete and recreate the "ESX Admins" group
and inherit full hypervisor administrative rights, because the hypervisor
never re-validated that the group's membership was the group it originally
trusted. Identity-plane trust and privileged-access trust are not the same
problem, and a governance program that solves the first without a distinct
answer for the second leaves exactly this gap open.

Concrete governance requirements this principle imposes, none of which the
identity-as-root architecture in §4 provides by itself:

1. **Privileged access is time-boxed and just-in-time**, not standing. A
   Global Admin or hypervisor-admin role held continuously is a
   continuously-available blast radius; granted for a bounded window against
   a specific, logged request, it is not.
2. **Break-glass accounts are governed artifacts, not an unwritten
   exception.** Every emergency-access path needs its own owner, its own
   monitoring, and its own periodic validation that it still requires
   emergency status — an undocumented break-glass account is a permanent,
   unaudited standing privilege wearing an excuse.
3. **Privileged-plane changes are independently verified, not
   self-attested.** The CVE-2024-37085 failure mode — trusting a security
   group's name without re-verifying its provenance — generalizes: any
   control that grants elevated access based on group membership, role
   assignment, or tag needs a mechanism confirming that membership was not
   itself attacker-created.
4. **Admin-plane telemetry is monitored as its own high-priority stream**,
   not folded into general device or identity logging where a
   privileged-access event is one line among thousands.

None of this substitutes for §4's identity-as-root architecture — it is the
answer to the question that architecture creates but does not itself
resolve: *if identity is the root, who is watching the root's own
administrators?*

### 6. Principle three — continuous evidence is a governance property, not a tool feature

CISA's Optimal maturity stage requires continuous, automated verification;
NIST SP 800-137 (*Information Security Continuous Monitoring*) and NIST
800-53's CA-7 control describe the same requirement as an ongoing program,
not a point-in-time assessment. CISA's [Binding Operational Directive
25-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-25-01-implementing-secure-practices-cloud-services)
operationalizes this for federal cloud services specifically: agencies must
not only assess Microsoft 365 configuration against the SCuBA baseline, they
must integrate that assessment with continuous-monitoring infrastructure and
**remediate deviations** on an ongoing basis — a scan report alone does not
satisfy the directive. **BOD 25-01's scope is M365-specific** — it does not
itself mandate continuous monitoring for a CSP's non-M365 workloads, an
agency's network boundary, or a VMware estate — but it is useful here as
evidence that "continuous, remediated" is already a live federal expectation
in at least one domain, not a novel or aspirational standard this paper is
inventing. §9 extends the *principle*, not the *directive's legal scope*, to
the rest of the whole-agency estate.

Evidence that actually supports Advanced/Optimal maturity has three
properties, none of which a single pillar tool produces on its own:

1. **Continuous** — captured as state changes occur, not on a periodic or
   audit-triggered cycle.
2. **Cross-pillar** — a single evidence record spans identity, device, and
   workload context rather than requiring an analyst to stitch together five
   tools' outputs by hand.
3. **Reproducible** — re-executable by an independent assessor without
   coordinating with the system operator, so the evidence on file matches
   what a re-run produces.

Governance is what makes these properties structural rather than
aspirational: it is the layer that defines a common evidence schema every
pillar tool's output is normalized into, assigns an owner for cross-pillar
correlation, and treats an open finding as either being actively remediated
or as a documented, dated, owned exception — never a silent gap. Absent that
governance layer, "continuous monitoring" collapses into "we ran the scan
again," which is Pattern 3 (§1) with a recurring calendar invite attached.

### 7. Principle four — governance sets policy; enforcement is what makes it stick

Every principle so far describes what governance should require. None of it
works if "governance" means only visibility and documentation. A program
that names an owner (§1, Pattern 1), detects drift (§1, Pattern 3), and files
an exception record has built a **detective** control — it can tell you,
after the fact, that something went wrong. It has not built a **preventive**
one, which stops the wrong thing from happening, or automatically contains
it, in the moment.

This distinction matters because the failure mode this paper spends its
first several sections describing — an agency that runs an assessment,
collects a finding, and never closes it — is exactly what a governance
program without enforcement teeth reproduces one layer up. "We have a
documented exception process" is not meaningfully different from "we ran the
scan again" (§1, Pattern 3) if the exception process has no expiry, no
automated re-check, and no mechanism that blocks the underlying condition
from recurring.

Concrete enforcement mechanisms a governance program has to include, not
merely the policies they enforce:

- **Preventive, not just detective, policy gates** — a cloud guardrail (a
  deny-effect policy, a service-control-policy boundary) that blocks a
  non-compliant resource from being created, not a scan that reports it
  after the fact.
- **Automated conditional blocking at the identity plane** — a policy that
  denies a sign-in outside declared risk parameters in real time, not a
  report that the sign-in occurred.
- **Hypervisor and infrastructure lockdown as a default posture**, not an
  optional hardening step — ESXi lockdown mode, restricted direct-console
  access, and verified (not name-trusted) AD-group provenance (§5) are
  enforcement, where a hardening checklist alone is documentation.
- **Time-bound exceptions that expire and re-trigger review automatically**
  — an exception without an expiry is a permanent, silent policy override
  wearing a governance label.

Governance that only observes is a more sophisticated version of the
assessment-without-remediation problem this whole paper argues against.
Governance that enforces is the difference between a maturity claim and an
actual control.

### 8. Principle five — the federal cloud boundary has to be modeled explicitly, not assumed away

Agencies operating in Microsoft's Government Community Cloud (GCC) — the
common FedRAMP Moderate-authorized federal case — inherit a structural
constraint that commercial Zero Trust guidance does not account for:
**feature availability narrows** relative to the commercial tier. Microsoft's
own service-description documentation for
[GCC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office365/servicedescriptions/office-365-platform-service-description/office-365-us-government/gcc)
documents this directly: new features ship to commercial tenants first and
reach GCC on a lag that sometimes runs months to years — and some
commercial-tier telemetry and analytics features never reach GCC at all.
(Higher government-community tiers exist above GCC for higher-impact
workloads; this paper is scoped to the FedRAMP Moderate / GCC case and does
not address them.) Independently, [TIC
3.0](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/programs/trusted-internet-connections-tic)
(per OMB M-19-26) imposes its own boundary-monitoring requirements on top of
whatever the cloud tier natively provides.

The governance principle: **an agency's Zero Trust maturity ceiling in a
given tier is a function of what that tier's telemetry actually exposes, and
that has to be assessed and documented, not assumed to match commercial
guidance.** Concretely, governance owes the program three things the cloud
tier alone does not provide:

1. **A capability-disposition inventory** — which pillar signals actually
   function in the agency's tier, verified directly, not inferred from
   commercial documentation.
2. **Explicit compensating controls** where a tier's native telemetry is
   absent — an agency-side mechanism that closes the gap, with the gap and
   its compensation both named in the authorization package rather than left
   implicit.
3. **A boundary posture treated as a first-class governed artifact** in the
   ATO documentation, not an assumption buried in a network diagram nobody
   re-validates.

Federal programs that skip this step routinely discover, at 3PAO review,
that their Zero Trust maturity claim for a pillar assumes telemetry their
tier does not actually deliver — a finding that is entirely avoidable with an
explicit capability inventory done up front.

### 9. Whole-agency scope: Network, CSPs, and VMware are one system, not three

Network, every CSP an agency operates, and any on-premises virtualization
estate have to resolve against the same naming and identity plane before a
"whole-agency" Zero Trust score means anything — three separate assessments
stapled together is not one assessment, it is three partial assessments
wearing one cover page. The hypervisor case is a distinct threat class, not
just a naming problem: ESXiArgs (CVE-2021-21974) and the ESXi AD-integration
bypass (CVE-2024-37085) both compromise a layer beneath every guest
workload's own telemetry, and vCenter's own identity domain is frequently
unfederated from the agency's broader identity plane. Once that unification
exists, it becomes the highest-value target in the estate in its own right
and needs the same privileged-access hardening as any other crown-jewel
system. The full argument — including the three architectural facts a
whole-agency program has to reconcile and the case for treating the
unification layer as a Tier-0 asset — is covered in *[Zero Trust Requires
Whole-Agency Scope](zero-trust-whole-agency-unification.qmd)*.

### 10. A worked example: why even Microsoft's own tools don't add up to "whole agency"

Even inside a single vendor's ecosystem, two complementary, free Microsoft
assessment tools — CISA's SCuBA/ScubaGear (a BOD 25-01-mandated M365
compliance check) and Microsoft's own Zero Trust Assessment (a broader
maturity check across Entra, Intune, Azure, and Purview) — overlap almost
entirely on identity and barely touch the same ground anywhere else, and
running both together still does not add up to a whole-agency answer.
That's because both tools are scoped to one vendor's platform:
agency-level Zero Trust ownership cannot be delegated to any single CSP's
assessment tool, however good. The full worked example, including practical
guidance for running SCuBA and the Zero Trust Assessment together, is
covered in *[Zero Trust Requires Whole-Agency
Scope](zero-trust-whole-agency-unification.qmd)*.

### 11. What maturity actually requires, pillar by pillar

**A note on sourcing, up front:** the table below is this paper's synthesis
of CISA's Advanced/Optimal criteria, phrased for readability. It is **not** a
verbatim quotation of the ZTMM v2.0 document and should not be cited as
CISA's exact language in a control crosswalk — consult the source document
directly for authoritative wording.

CISA's own Advanced/Optimal criteria, read pillar by pillar, are consistently
about continuous, automated, identity-anchored behavior rather than a bigger
tool:

| Pillar | What "Advanced/Optimal" requires (per CISA ZTMM v2.0, paraphrased) | The governance dependency |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | Continuous validation, phishing-resistant authentication, dynamic risk-based access decisions | Requires identity to be the addressing root (§4) other pillars resolve against — and its own root-of-trust hardened per §4–§5 |
| **Devices** | Continuous, real-time device compliance and vulnerability visibility with automated response | Requires cross-pillar correlation (§3, via Automation and Orchestration) between device posture and identity/workload context |
| **Networks** | Distributed micro-segmentation, encrypted traffic, dynamic policy enforcement | Requires network policy to be *derived from* identity/workload context, not independently administered (§4), and enforced preventively, not just observed (§7) |
| **Applications & Workloads** | Continuous authorization, immutable workloads, application-level micro-segmentation | Requires workload identity to resolve against the same identity plane as users and devices |
| **Data** | Continuous data inventory, automated categorization, and dynamic access control tied to data sensitivity | Requires the evidence properties in §6 — cross-pillar, continuous, reproducible — to actually classify and track data at the pace access decisions require |

Every row's Advanced/Optimal criterion depends on a cross-cutting capability,
not a bigger pillar-specific tool. This is the structural reason "buy a
better tool for the pillar we're weakest in" does not move the maturity
needle the way agencies expect it to.

### 12. Tools agencies already have: mapping remediation to what's already licensed

§7 argued governance needs enforcement, not just visibility; §5 argued
privileged and administrative identity need controls of their own. Both are
routinely treated as if they required new procurement. For most federal
agencies they don't — much of what those two principles call for is already
sitting, unconfigured, inside two platforms most agencies have already
licensed for other purposes, plus native tooling inside every major CSP's
government-authorized tier. What follows is an inventory check, not a
product endorsement: before budgeting for a gap, confirm whether the
capability already exists in something already paid for.

**ServiceNow — the workflow/orchestration layer.** ServiceNow's Government
Community Cloud is authorized at a level that meets FedRAMP Moderate
requirements. (Naming collision worth flagging: ServiceNow calls its own
environment "GCC" too, distinct from Microsoft's GCC tier in §8 — confirm
which "GCC" a given document means.) Two specific mappings:

- §7's "time-bound exceptions that expire and re-trigger review
  automatically" is what a workflow/GRC platform's ticketing and
  exception-lifecycle modules exist to do — an exception with an assigned
  owner, an expiry date, and an automated re-open trigger is exactly §7's
  governance-as-enforcement, provided those fields are actually populated
  and the automation actually runs. The platform supplies the mechanism, not
  the discipline.
- §6's requirement for "a common evidence schema every pillar tool's output
  is normalized into" describes exactly the role a workflow platform can
  play as the cross-pillar evidence and correlation-owner home Pattern 1
  (§1) says is missing — again, only if it's actually configured that way,
  not simply licensed.

**SailPoint — the identity-governance layer.** SailPoint Identity Security
Cloud holds a FedRAMP Moderate ATO (325 controls, hosted on AWS GovCloud),
with FedRAMP-authorized add-ons for Non-Employee Risk Management and Data
Access Security. This maps directly onto §4 (identity as the addressing
root) and, more specifically, §5 (privileged and administrative identity):
identity governance and administration platforms are built for periodic
access certification, separation-of-duties enforcement, and third-party/
non-employee identity risk — the product category *is* §5's "privileged
access is time-boxed" and "privileged-plane changes are independently
verified" requirements, if certification campaigns are actually scoped to
catch group-membership drift (the CVE-2024-37085 failure mode, §2) and not
just initial provisioning.

**Native CSP tooling.** Every major CSP ships a policy-enforcement
mechanism and a posture/drift-detection tool inside its government-authorized
tier:

| CSP | Preventive enforcement | Posture / drift detection | Government-tier FedRAMP status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft Azure | Azure Policy (deny-effect guardrails) | Microsoft Defender for Cloud | Azure Government: authorized at a level meeting FedRAMP Moderate; Azure Policy ships a FedRAMP-Moderate-mapped built-in initiative |
| AWS | Service Control Policies (AWS Organizations) | AWS Security Hub | AWS GovCloud (US): authorized at a level meeting FedRAMP Moderate; Security Hub is in scope |
| Google Cloud | Organization Policy Service / VPC Service Controls | Security Command Center | Assured Workloads: authorized services (including Security Command Center) meet FedRAMP Moderate per Google's own guidance |
| Oracle Cloud Infrastructure | OCI IAM policies | Cloud Guard | Oracle Cloud for Government: authorized at a level meeting FedRAMP Moderate; Cloud Guard is in scope |

Each of these is a real, verified, government-authorized mechanism for
exactly the preventive-enforcement pattern §7 calls for — **within its own
platform.** None of the four reconciles across CSPs, the network layer, or a
VMware estate, which is precisely §9's and §10's point generalized past
Microsoft's ecosystem: a CSP's native tool is scoped to what that CSP can
see. ServiceNow and SailPoint are the two tool classes actually positioned
to span the silos, because workflow orchestration and identity governance
are not CSP-native categories — but neither is a substitute for the
naming/asset reconciliation §9 requires. They are the enforcement and
governance layer that sits *on top of* that reconciliation once it exists,
not the reconciliation itself.

**Two verification caveats, not a substitute for reading the ATO package:**
FedRAMP authorization is per-service and per-region — a vendor meeting
Moderate requirements somewhere does not mean every feature, in every
region, is inside a given agency's own authorization boundary; confirm the
specific service is named in the system's own inheritance package. And a tool being licensed and
authorized is not the same as it being configured for the purpose described
here — the same governance-vs-enforcement gap in §7 applies to whether a
ServiceNow exception record actually expires or a SailPoint certification
campaign actually runs on schedule, not just whether the platform is present.

### 13. What an agency can do this quarter

Concrete, vendor-agnostic governance steps, in order of leverage:

1. **Inventory which pillar evidence is actually reproducible today.** For
   each ZTMM pillar, can an independent assessor re-run the evidence pipeline
   without coordinating with your operations staff? Where the answer is no,
   that is where governance investment should go first — not into another
   pillar tool.
2. **Name an owner for cross-pillar correlation.** Pattern 1 (§1) persists as
   long as no one is accountable for reconciling identity, device, and
   workload signals against each other. This is an organizational decision,
   not a procurement.
3. **Stand up continuous drift detection as a governance function**, not a
   per-tool feature — even a manual quarterly reconciliation between declared
   policy and observed configuration is a structural improvement over
   discovering drift at audit time (Pattern 3, §1).
4. **Model your cloud boundary explicitly.** If operating in GCC or an
   equivalent FedRAMP Moderate government-community tier, produce the
   capability-disposition inventory described in §8 before claiming a
   maturity stage that assumes commercial-tier telemetry your tier does not
   deliver.
5. **Reconcile Network, CSP, and VMware asset identity to one authoritative
   source before scoring any of them — and treat that unified source as a
   Tier-0 asset in its own right (§9).** If the network team, the cloud
   security team, and the virtualization team cannot point to the same
   authoritative naming/asset record for a given workload, the "whole-agency"
   score is not measuring one architecture; once they can, the unification
   layer itself needs the same privileged-access hardening as any other
   crown-jewel system.
6. **Assign agency-level ownership of the Zero Trust posture, separate from
   any CSP relationship.** Per §10, no CSP's native assessment tool — however
   good — is scoped to see past its own platform. If the only place your
   Zero Trust posture is "owned" is inside each CSP's own console or report,
   no one is actually accountable for the agency-wide picture; name that
   owner explicitly.
7. **Convert at least one detective control into a preventive one this
   quarter.** Per §7, pick the single highest-leverage drift finding your
   program currently only documents, and wire in an automated block — a
   deny-effect cloud policy, a Conditional Access rule, ESXi lockdown mode —
   rather than adding it to next quarter's remediation list again.
8. **Put privileged and administrative access under time-boxed,
   independently-verified control**, per §5 — starting with whichever admin
   plane (identity, hypervisor, or CSP management account) currently has the
   most standing, non-expiring access.

None of these requires a multi-year program or a new procurement. Each is a
governance decision that compounds — and each is exactly the kind of
investment the "Governance" cross-cutting capability in CISA's own model
calls for.

### 14. Honest limits

- CISA's ZTMM does not prescribe *how* to implement the three cross-cutting
  capabilities — the principles above are one architecturally sound reading
  of the model's Advanced/Optimal criteria, not the only path.
- The capability-disposition work in §8 is tenant-specific: Microsoft's
  service descriptions establish that feature availability narrows in GCC
  relative to commercial in general, but don't substitute for an agency
  verifying its own tenant's actual telemetry.
- "Continuous" evidence (§6) is a target property, not a claim every agency
  can reach immediately — the honest first step is usually identifying which
  pillar evidence is *not yet* reproducible.
- The whole-agency argument (§9) is architectural, not an integration design.
  Which CSPs and hypervisor platform an agency runs, and how exactly to
  unify their naming and asset identity, are per-agency engineering
  decisions this paper doesn't prescribe.
- The SCuBA / Zero Trust Assessment comparison (§10) is a
  Microsoft-ecosystem worked example, not a universal claim about every
  CSP's tooling — the overlap percentages are specific to those two tools;
  only the "can't delegate ownership to a vendor's tool" principle
  generalizes.
- The incidents cited (§2, §4, §5, §9) are illustrative, not a threat
  catalogue — a real program's threat model should come from its own risk
  assessment. And this paper doesn't cover OT/ICS or mainframe estates,
  which many agencies also operate and to which the ZTMM pillars apply
  differently.
- The FedRAMP authorization statuses in §12 are a snapshot, verified at the
  time of writing, of specific named products (ServiceNow Government
  Community Cloud, SailPoint Identity Security Cloud, and each CSP's
  government-authorized tier). Authorization scope changes as vendors add
  services and renew ATOs; confirm current status against FedRAMP's own
  marketplace listing before relying on it, and treat §12's tool mapping as
  a starting inventory, not an audit finding.

### 15. Conclusion

CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model is frequently read as a five-pillar
checklist. Read correctly, it's a five-pillar model **operated through**
three cross-cutting capabilities, and Governance is the one federal programs
invest in least and need most to reach Advanced or Optimal maturity.

The principles in this paper follow one thread: identity is a necessary
anchor, not a self-authenticating one — which is exactly why its
administrators, its evidence trail, its enforcement, its cloud boundary, and
its reach across Network, CSPs, and VMware all need governing in their own
right, not just the identity assertion itself. None of that is a product to
buy. It's what CISA's model already requires — read in full, and read
against how these architectures actually fail in practice — of any program
serious about the *whole* agency, rather than a horse somewhere behind a
cart that already left.
